items.title: New Congress, New Rare Earths Policy?
items.content: Two announcements before we dive in: Remember when Jordan’s wife ran a ‘looking for a CTO’ post for an insuretech startup? Well, thanks to the ChinaTalk network, she found an incredible one . They’re now revenue positive and halfway through a seed round. Thank you all for the help! Jordan will be in DC the week after Thanksgiving for a hot minute and will be hosting a meetup on Dec 2nd. This piece was authored by anonymous contributor “Matteo Clavijero”. The blue wave of the midterms has put rare earth companies in the hot seat. Rare earths, particularly those used in the production of permanent magnets, are a critical input enabling trillions of dollars of downstream economic value. Beijing dominates the rare earth magnet supply chain from ore extraction to magnetization, with over 90% of mining, refining, and magnet-making concentrated in China. The CCP has repeatedly sought geopolitical leverage by exercising export restrictions on rare earths to constrict Western economies, and American rare earth competitors have been supported by industrial policy in response. After all, without rare earths the production of a laundry list of technologies — EVs, data centers, drones, wind turbines, smartphones, robots, and more — grinds to a halt. The US has been attempting to support an ex-China rare earth industry for the past decade, and government support is necessary for any ex-China industry to succeed. Projects are low-margin, decade-long investments that require the government to derisk and backstop ventures, such that the barriers to success are low enough that private investment takes the industry seriously. The second Trump administration has made a flurry of deals, replete with debt financing and equity purchases from the Export-Import Bank (EXIM) and the Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), ostensibly for the purpose of securing America’s critical mineral supply chains. But many deals h…

items.title: MOFCOM's New Rules: Digging For Leverage
items.content: With the world scrambling to diffuse China’s rare earth weapon, Chinese regulators have apparently been tasked with identifying alternative sources of potential leverage. MOFCOM’s recent work created legal mechanisms to restrict the flow of a curious collection of products: tunnel boring machines, dredging components, solar manufacturing equipment, biotechnology, and drones. At first glance, this seems like an eclectic list, but these technologies are connected beyond the fact that they are all made in China. Today, we’re unpacking the geopolitical incentives that made them MOFCOM’s business. This is part two of our series on MOFCOM’s October 2026 regulatory drops. In part one, we analyzed the October 16th proposals for regulating AI technologies. Today’s installment tackles the October 16th proposals for biotech and solar and the mixed bag from October 19th. We explore: Why parsing China’s trade policy requires looking beyond the US-China rivalry to Beijing’s bilateral relations with other capitals — and why India in particular is under fire; How tunnel boring machines and dredgers help us understand China’s ambitions as a regional power; Beijing’s playbook for keeping foreign countries dependent on its solar provisions; And, what biotech and drones tell us about China’s approach to intellectual property. ChinaTalk is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. items.title: Jensen Out, MATCH Act In?
items.content: Jordan Schneider, Dylan Patel, and Jordan Nanos of SemiAnalysis record an emergency pod after Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO. We discuss: Why Jensen’s exit could become cover for “really stupid laws” — and why Dylan backs the MATCH Act but thinks RASA is a mistake. The game theory of remote access: renting compute to Chinese firms as margin capture and a kill switch, versus closing the Malaysia loophole outright. “Flip the table”: why equipment controls beat chip and model controls, and how close Huawei’s silicon now is. Why no American lab has out-built Kimi or DeepSeek in open models. Nvidia without Jensen: talent retention, Rubin and Feynman execution risk, and who should run the company. Colette Kress’s exposure, Supermicro and Megaspeed, and a fight over whether this amounts to the “nationalization” of Nvidia. Listen now on your favorite podcast app . items.title: Notion’s Founder on the One Thing Your AI Is Missing
items.content: Everybody can start making their own software, no? In some sense, the original vision of the 60s, 70s, hippie generation of computing come to life, and that's actually why Notion was started. Notion was about how do we bring this computing power to as many people as possible without forcing them to learn how to code. Hello and welcome to the Every Podcast. I'm Dan Shipper. And I'm Natalia Quintero. And this week we're talking about a conversation that you had, Dan, with Ivan Zhao, CEO and founder of Notion. Can you tell me a little bit about what you learned? Yeah, it was such an interesting conversation because Notion is the original, one of the original no code companies. The way it's structured with databases and forms and blocks, it's all designed to allow you to build something that looks kind of like software without knowing how to code. But AI like totally changed that. Now anyone can Vibe code whatever they want. You don't really need a block system. You don't really need the whole Notion interface in order to make something that looks like software. And so it kind of forced them to reinvent what they are and reinvent or rethink the original vision for their product. I've been a user of Notion for a long time, and the product has evolved quite a bit. What do you think makes Ivan the right leader to lead this transformation? You know him well. Ivan is one of those interesting people. I think there's some kind of soul overlap between Notion and Every, and I think that comes from who Ivan is as a person. You know, the way that he dresses and the way that they furnish their office, and there's so much attention to detail and so much craft in what they do. And I think that that's actually sorely missing from the... pantheon of AI CEOs. Like when you really think about what kinds of CEOs are around in this era, there are very few people who care a lot about the details and the feeling of work and what you make. And especially in a world where everyone's afraid of AI taking jobs and how do you keep the work that we do feeling human or feeling special. I think that there's something really interesting happening with Notion and Ivan is the right person to make that happen. So if you didn't catch it at thesis, let's turn over now to a conversation between Dan Shipper and Ivan Zao from Notion. Welcome, really excited to have you here. Good to be here. And I was like, I don't know, but next time, we'll make it bigger if you want to pay a little more. It's big enough. Good love. Great. Nice to be here. So in addition to sponsoring this conference, you make Notion. And I think of you as, we were talking about this a little bit backstage. I think there is a spiritual similarity between the way that Notion and every think about work. And I think that comes from you specifically. you think a lot about the craft of work and thinking well with software. And I think when we are, like in AI there seems like there's this bifurcation between people who think it's all slop and people who think that you can actually do good work with it. And I'm curious like how you're thinking about this as you're bringing Notion into this era and in your own life. We're probably in the one year after the Vibe coding phase at this point, for most people. Probably in this room. A year ago, people say software is dead, Vibe code everything. Then nine months ago, people realized you need to maintain them. I'm actually in different directions. I love the spirit of Vibe coding. Actually, if anything, Vibe coding, the spirit is the spirit that YNOTION was started in the first place. I think so, right? Yeah. If I share this with you all, it's... items.title: Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs
items.content: Happy to bring to you our episode with Black Forest Labs. Our guests today are Andreas Blattmann, he also goes by Andi, who is co-inventor of latent diffusion, the technique that eventually got scaled up by Stable Diffusion and Stability AI, and they eventually split with a bunch of, uh, the core Stability AI image gen folks to form Black Forest Labs. And Dustin Podell, who I also met with Anj, uh, at one of the stories that we tell, and, uh, who worked his way up from just being a regular engineer, a freelance, like, web developer person, into a model and research lead at Stability AI, and now, uh, Black Forest Labs, creator of SDXL, Control LoRA, post-training lead on SD3, Flux Ultra, Flux.1, and Flux Context. And we go into all of these details. Um, as you may know, sometimes we're very honored to have an extended history with some of our guests, and this is one of them. You might have heard in our Anj Mittal episode where we talked about introducing each other at one of the NeurIPS's [smacks lips] and meeting Black Forest Labs for the first time. And, uh, this was right after Stable Diffusion. But what you may not have heard, and we only tell this story in this episode, is how latent space itself was started because of Stable Diffusion, directly, uh, crediting the launch for me basically quitting my job to go all in on AI based on what we saw. And today's guest, Dustin, also [chuckles] had that experience, and so did Vibhu. And so we have a very, very strong tie with the team that basically led up to Black Forest Labs, and now we're also interested in what's next for them. Like, they have created some of the best open and closed weights models for image generation and video generation. I think especially Flux Context, if you're not aware of image editing models, I do think that this is in the ex-in the limit one of the things to fully replace Canva and, um, and Photoshop and a bunch of other workflows and editors that you might use in a normal creative workflow. It is not going to replace the top end of the market. But for regular, normal, everyday edits, why would you not want anything else other than to query a model and ask it to do, uh, image editing for you? Uh, we do this obviously with this kind of video editing. It's all Clanker done, and I do review it, and they're also moving into robotics. And so this ties in with a miniseries of model labs that have been pursuing this direction, building world models from image gen, like with Runway, uh, as well as, um, video models and now robotics models. And so I think a lot of things rhyme in a lot of our recent episodes, like even the artificial analysis episode that we're gonna release soon, they are also going into robotics, and, like, it seems pretty s- obvious that when you see a whole bunch of smart people who are at the frontier all leaning one direction, that you're probably six to 12 months out from some kind of really big breakthrough. This has been a consistent theme over my last four years of podcasting. It's not gonna change now. So look out for it. Um, that's the [chuckles] most obvious call-out I can make. But there's also a lot of interesting lore for people interested in the general diffusion space. Uh, we're gonna d- do a little bit more over time. I, I'm thinking about an AI- AIE LA, where we talk about the generative media field and the creative arts and how, uh, that complicated relationship is evolving, um, and I think maturing, to be honest. And finally, for those longtime listeners, uh, we are starting to open up to advertisers, people that we really admire and respect and wanna showcase what they're working on. Um, the first one was with Supabase, which I think a lot of you enjoyed, and the second one today is brought to you by Deepgram, and you'll hear more from us at the midpoint of the episode. [upbeat music] You should be showing a robot an action one time, and then it should be able to do this, and this would be truly a superhuman intelligence…

items.title: Piggybacking to the Frontier
items.content: American data companies like Mercor, Surge AI, AfterQuery, and Turing are selling roughly half a billion dollars worth of data to Chinese AI labs. A chunk of that data comes in the form of reinforcement learning (RL) environments, which labs use to post-train their models to make them excel at specific domains like coding, cyber, finance, law, and bio. Post-training, and especially RL, is one of the most important indicators of the final performance of a model. Whenever a new model within a single generation drops, the advances from the previous release are entirely due to post-training. The difference between Opus 5 to Opus 5.5, or from GPT 5.5 to GPT 5.6, is not due to a new pre-training run. Since they have the same base model, the capability gains come from researchers teaching the model to get better at specific domains. The phenomenon of American companies arming Chinese labs with the data that enables this RL should set off alarms for policymakers and those invested in the U.S.-China AI race: American companies are helping Chinese labs develop better models, and we were able to find at least nine who do so. But the business relationships between data vendors and Chinese labs are more complicated than that single hawkish line, and today, we’re diving into what’s going on. We’ll cover: What it means to sell an RL environment and how it differs from distillation The current ecosystem of China-tied data vendors To what extent American companies are selling RL environments to China Whether this is a problem that needs fixing What RL Does and Doesn’t Look Like Example RL Flows RL environments are essentially simulated worlds in which a model can train to improve its performance at specific tasks or environments. As an example, a model developer may want their model to get better at creating PowerPoint slides with pleasant aesthetics and clear text. To achieve that capability, the model developer may go to a data vendor and ask them to make…

Please please subscribe here to support ChinAI under a Guardian /Wikipedia-style tipping model (everyone gets the same content but those who can pay support access for all AND compensation for awesome ChinAI contributors). items.title: Korea’s Stock Market Crashed $1 Trillion. What Does That Mean for the Global AI Race?
items.content: Richard Gray is an analyst who works for a foreign policy think tank in Washington, D.C. Since 2025, South Korea’s capital markets have vacillated from the world’s best-performing to shedding more than $1 trillion in market capitalization. This volatility is a story of how Korea’s financial system overlays supply chain specialization. With Korean firms Samsung and SK hynix controlling a majority share of global memory, South Korea’s stock market functionally operates as a single, highly leveraged node within the AI financial architecture. Two interwoven dynamics explain the convulsions of Korean capital markets and their global ramifications. The first is the Korea discount , in which Korean equities are structurally undervalued because of lagging financial development and weak corporate governance. The second is a memory discount , with each leading high-bandwidth memory (HBM) company (Micron in the U.S., SK hynix and Samsung in Korea) having depressed valuations in their respective markets. The June-July 2026 crash rippled far beyond Korea’s borders and forewarns what may be to come in future market corrections. For Korea, its historically shallow capital markets and exposure to the memory sector — which is now facing emergent Chinese competitors — serve as overlapping pressures on its financial position. In this environment, the threat of a market correction cascading across global markets and the U.S.-China tech competition looms large. The Zenith: Capital Infusion The Korean market is essentially a bet on two companies competing in the same industry. Korea’s memory chip industry has driven exponential year-on-year growth in Korea’s capital markets. From March 2025 to June 2026, the KOSPI — Korea’s main stock index — rose 241%, adding nearly $3.3 trillion in capitalization and exceeding the total increase accumulated over the index’s 43-year history (Bloomberg). In June 2026, SK, Sams…
